## XVI.4 Topological Algebras

We extend the definitions of algebras, quasi-bialgebras, etc. to the setting of $\mathbf{C}[[h]]$ -modules. This is done by replacing the algebraic tensor product of II.1 by the topological tensor product of Section 3.

A topological algebra is a triple $(A, \mu ,\eta)$ where $A$ is a module over the ring $K = \mathbf{C}[[h]]$, $\mu : A\widetilde{\otimes} A \to A$ and $\eta : K \to A$ are $K$-linear maps such that

$$
\mu \circ (\mu \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}) = \mu \circ (\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \mu)
$$

(4.1)

and

$$
\mu \circ (\eta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}) = \mathrm {i d} _ {A} = \mu \circ (\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \eta).
$$

(4.2)

As in the algebraic case, we use the convention

$$
a a ^ {\prime} = \mu \left(a \widetilde {\otimes} a ^ {\prime}\right)
$$

(4.3)

for the product of two elements a, $a^{\prime}$ of a topological algebra (A, $\mu,\eta).$ We also write 1 for the image under $\eta$ of the unit element 1 of K.

Let $( A, \mu, \eta)$ be a topological algebra and $f(h)=\sum_{n\geq0} c_n h^n$ be a formal series with complex coefficients. For an element $a\in A$ , the formula

$$
f (h a) = \sum_ {n \geq 0} c _ {n} a ^ {n} h ^ {n}
$$

(4.4)

$$
f (h a) = \sum_ {n \geq 0} c _ {n} a ^ {n} h ^ {n}
$$

(4.4)

defines a unique element in the inverse limit $\widetilde{A}=\varprojlim_{n} A / h^{n} A$ . Therefore if $A$ is separated and complete, it defines an element, still denoted $f(ha)$ , in $A\cong \widetilde{A}$ . This procedure can be applied to the classical exponential function $e^{h}=\sum_{n>0}\frac{h^{n}}{n!}$ , yielding elements of the form

$$
e ^ {h a} = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \frac {a ^ {n} h ^ {n}}{n !}
$$

(4.5)

in any separated complete topological algebra A. If $a^{\prime}$ is another element in A commuting with a, then

$$
e ^ {h a} e ^ {h a ^ {\prime}} = e ^ {h \left(a + a ^ {\prime}\right)}.
$$

(4.6)

As a consequence, we see that $e^{ha}$ is invertible in A with inverse equal to $e^{-ha}.$

A morphism $f : (A, \mu , \eta) \rightarrow (A^{\prime}, \mu^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime})$ of topological algebras is a $K$-linear map $f : A \rightarrow A^{\prime}$ such that

$$
f \circ \mu = \mu^ {\prime} \circ \left(f \widetilde {\otimes} f\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad f \circ \eta = \eta^ {\prime}.
$$

(4.7)

Using the convention of (4.3), Relations (4.7) can be rewritten as

$$
f \left(a _ {1} a _ {2}\right) = f \left(a _ {1}\right) f \left(a _ {2}\right) \quad \text {a n d} \quad f (1) = 1
$$

(4.8)

A topological quasi-bialgebra is a sextuple $( A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, \Phi)$ where $( A, \mu, \eta)$ is a topological algebra, $\Delta : A \to A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ and $\varepsilon : A \to K$ are K-linear maps, and $\Phi$ is an invertible element of the tensor product algebra $A\widetilde{\otimes} A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ such that

$$
\left(\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \Delta\right) (\Delta (a)) = \Phi \left(\left(\Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) (\Delta (a))\right) \Phi^ {- 1}
$$

(4.10)

for all a $\in A$

$$
(\varepsilon \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}) \Delta = \mathrm {i d} _ {A} = (\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \varepsilon) \Delta ,
$$

(4.11)

$$
\left(\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \Delta\right) (\Phi) \left(\Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) (\Phi) = \Phi_ {2 3 4} \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) (\Phi) \Phi_ {1 2 3},
$$

$$

(4.13)

When $\Phi = 1\widetilde{\otimes}1\widetilde{\otimes}1$ , we call A a topological bialgebra.

A morphism $f : ( A, \mu , \eta , \Delta , \varepsilon , \Phi) \rightarrow ( A^{\prime}, \mu^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}, \Delta^{\prime}, \varepsilon^{\prime}, \Phi^{\prime})$ of topological quasi-bialgebras is a morphism $f$ between the underlying topological algebras such that

$$
(f \widetilde {\otimes} f) \Delta = \Delta^ {\prime} f \quad \text {a n d} \quad (f \widetilde {\otimes} f \widetilde {\otimes} f) (\Phi) = \Phi^ {\prime}.
$$

(4.14)

A topological quasi-bialgebra $( A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, \Phi)$ is a topological braided quasi-bialgebra if there exists an invertible element R of the tensor product algebra $A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ such that

$$
\Delta^ {\mathrm {o p}} (a) = R \Delta (a) R ^ {- 1},
$$

(4.15)

$$
\left(\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \Delta\right) (R) = \left(\Phi_ {2 3 1}\right) ^ {- 1} R _ {1 3} \Phi_ {2 1 3} R _ {1 2} \left(\Phi_ {1 2 3}\right) ^ {- 1},
$$

(4.16)

\left(\Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) (R) = \Phi_ {3 1 2} R _ {1 3} \left(\Phi_ {1 3 2}\right) ^ {- 1} R _ {2 3} \Phi_ {1 2 3}.
$$

(4.17)

As before, $R$ is called the universal $R$ -matrix of $A.$ It is part of the data of a topological braided quasi-bialgebra. A morphism of topological braided

quasi-bialgebras is a morphism of the underlying topological quasi-bialgebras sending the universal R-matrix of the first one to the universal R-matrix of the second one.

We also need the concept of a gauge transformation on a topological quasi-bialgebra A: it is an invertible element F of $A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ such that

$$
(\varepsilon \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}) (F) = (\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \varepsilon) (F) = 1.
$$

(4.18)

From a topological (braided) quasi-bialgebra $A$ and a gauge transformation F one can form a new topological (braided) quasi-bialgebra $A_{F}$ by (XV.3.2- 3.3) and (XV.3.9).

Example 3. Let $A_{0}=\left( A_{0}, \mu_{0}, \eta_{0}, \Delta_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}, \Phi_{0}, R_{0} \right)$ be a braided quasi-bialgebra over the field C of complex numbers. Using Proposition 2.3 (b) and Proposition 3.2, one may define the topological braided quasi-bialgebra

$$
A _ {0} [ [ h ] ] = \left(A _ {0} [ [ h ] ], \mu , \eta , \Delta , \varepsilon , \Phi_ {0}, R _ {0}\right)
$$

on the space of formal series with coefficients in $A_{0}$ where $\mu, \eta, \Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are the unique K-linear maps such that $\eta ( f )=f\eta_{0} ( 1 )=f1$ for all $f\in K$

$$
\mu \left(a \widetilde {\otimes} a ^ {\prime}\right) = \mu_ {0} \left(a \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right), \quad \Delta (a) = \Delta_ {0} (a), \quad \varepsilon (a) = \varepsilon_ {0} (a)
$$

for all $a,a^{\prime}\in A_{0}.$ We call $A_{0}[[h]]$ the trivial topological braided quasibialgebra associated to $A_{0}.$

Example 4. Let $A = (A, \mu ,\eta ,\Delta ,\varepsilon ,\Phi ,R)$ be a topological braided quasibialgebra. Since $( A \widetilde{\otimes} A ) / h ( A \widetilde{\otimes} A ) \cong A / h A \otimes A / h A$ , the K-linear maps $\mu, \eta ,\Delta ,\varepsilon$ induce C-linear maps

$$
\bar {\mu}: A / h A \otimes A / h A \rightarrow A / h A, \quad \bar {\eta}: \mathbf {C} \rightarrow A / h A,
$$

$$
\bar {\Delta}: A / h A \rightarrow A / h A \otimes A / h A, \quad \bar {\varepsilon}: A / h A \rightarrow \mathbf {C}.
$$

Define $\bar{\Phi}$ as the class of $\Phi$ modulo $(A / h A)^{\otimes 3}$ and $\bar{R}$ as the class of $R$ modulo $(A / h A)^{\otimes 2}$ . Then $\bar{A}=\left(A / h A,\bar{\mu},\bar{\eta},\bar{\Delta},\bar{\varepsilon},\bar{\Phi},\bar{R}\right)$ is a braided quasi-bialgebra.

Another concept we need to adapt is the concept of a topological A-module M over a topological algebra $A = (A, \mu ,\eta)$ . It is a left K-module with a K-linear map $\mu_{M}:A\widetilde{\otimes} M\to M$ such that

$$
\mu_ {M} \circ (\widetilde {\mu} \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {M}) = \mu_ {M} \circ (\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \mu_ {M}) \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad \mu_ {M} \circ (\eta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {M}) = \mathrm {i d} _ {M}.
$$

(4.19)

We shall write $\mu_{M} ( a\widetilde{\otimes} m )=am$ for $a\in A$ and $m\in M.$ The definition of a morphism of topological A-modules is left to the reader.

Let M and N be topological A-modules. Then their topological tensor product $M\widetilde{\otimes} N$ is a topological $A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ -module. If A has a comultiplication $\Delta :A\to A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ , we can pull back the $A\widetilde{\otimes} A$ -module structure on $M\widetilde{\otimes} N$ to a topological A-module structure given by

$$
a \left(m \widetilde {\otimes} n\right) = \Delta (a) \left(m \widetilde {\otimes} n\right)
$$

(4.20)

for all $a\in A, m$ in M, and n in N.

## XVI.5 Quantum Enveloping Algebras

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex Lie algebra. In V.2 we defined its enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ and proved that it had a natural bialgebra structure determined by

$$
\Delta (x) = 1 \otimes x + x \otimes 1 \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad \varepsilon (x) = 0
$$

for all x belonging to $\mathfrak{g}$ . We equip it with a trivial braided quasi-bialgebra structure with $\Phi=1\otimes 1\otimes 1$ and $R=1\otimes 1.$

Definition XVI.5.1. A quantum enveloping algebra (QUE) for the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is a topological braided quasi-bialgebra $A=(A,\mu ,\eta ,\Delta ,\varepsilon ,\Phi ,R)$ such that A is a topologically free module, the induced braided quasi-bialgebra $\bar{A}=(A/hA,\bar{\mu},\bar{\eta},\bar{\Delta},\varepsilon ,\Phi ,\bar{R})$ as in Example 4 of Section 4 coincides with the trivial braided quasi-bialgebra structure of $U(\mathfrak{g})$ and the map $\eta$ is trivially extended from $\bar{\eta}.$

Let us be more explicit about this definition. First, a QUE is topologically free. This means that $A = (A / h A)[[h]]$ as a left K-module. By hypothesis, we also have $A / h A = U(\mathfrak{g})$

$$
A = U (\mathfrak {g}) [ [ h ] ]
$$

Therefore

A ^ {\widetilde {\otimes} n} = \left(U (\mathfrak {g}) ^ {\otimes n}\right) [ [ h ] ]
$$

(5.2)

$$

(5.3)

where $(\mu_{n})_{n\geq 0}$ is a family of linear maps from $U(\mathfrak{g})\otimes U(\mathfrak{g})$ to $U(\mathfrak{g})$ such that $\mu_{0}$ is the product in the enveloping algebra. Similarly,

$$

\varepsilon (a) = \sum_ {n > 0} \varepsilon_ {n} (a) h ^ {n}
$$

$$

(5.5)

where $(\varepsilon_{n})_{n\geq 0}$ is a family of linear maps from $U(\mathfrak{g})$ to C such that $\varepsilon_{0}$ is the counit of the enveloping algebra. The last part of Definition 5.1 means that the unit $\eta$ of A is given by

$$
\eta (f) = f 1
$$

(5.6)

for all $f\in \mathbf{C}[[h]]$ . Finally, by Proposition 3.2 again, the elements $\Phi$ and R can be written

$$
\Phi = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \Phi_ {n} h ^ {n}

(5.7)

and

R = \sum_ {n \geq 0} R _ {n} h ^ {n}

(5.8)

where $(\Phi_{n})_{n\geq 0}$ and $(R_{n})_{n\geq 0}$ are families of elements of $U(\mathfrak{g})^{\otimes 3}$ and $U(\mathfrak{g})^{\otimes 2}$ respectively such that

\Phi_ {0} = 1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1 \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad R _ {0} = 1 \otimes 1.
$$

(5.9)

It is clear from Lemma 1.1 that (5.9) ensures the invertibility of $\Phi$ and $R.$

By definition, a quantum enveloping algebra $A$ is associated to a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}.$ One recovers $\mathfrak{g}$ from $A$ by

$$
\mathfrak {g} = \left\{x \in A / h A \mid \Delta_ {0} (a) = 1 \otimes a + a \otimes 1 \right\}
$$

(5.10)

in view of the fact (stated in V.9) that the subspace of primitive elements in $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is $\mathfrak{g}$ provided that the ground field is of characteristic zero.

We now associate another invariant to a QUE A. If R is its universal $R$ - matrix and $R_{21}$ is the image of R under the flip, the formula

$$
R _ {2 1} R \equiv 1 \otimes 1 + h t \pmod {h ^ {2}}
$$

(5.11)

defines a unique element $t\in U(\mathfrak{g})\otimes U(\mathfrak{g})$ . Expressing t using (5.8), we get $t=R_{1}+(R_{1})_{2 1}$ , which immediately proves that

$$
t _ {2 1} = t.
$$

(5.12)

Proposition XVI.5.2. The element t is an invariant symmetric element of $\mathfrak{g}\otimes\mathfrak{g}$ , i.e., we have $t_{21}=t$ and $[\Delta(x),t]=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{g}$ . It remains unchanged under any gauge transformation.

The element $t \in \mathfrak{g} \otimes\mathfrak{g}$ will be referred to as the canonical 2-tensor of the quantum enveloping algebra A. Drinfeld calls the pair $(\mathfrak{g}, t)$ the classical limit of A and the quantum enveloping algebra A a quantization of the pair $(\mathfrak{g}, t).$

Proof. We have already observed that $t$ is symmetric. Let us prove that it belongs to the subspace $\mathfrak{g}\otimes\mathfrak{g}$ . We again use the fact that $\mathfrak{g}$ is the subspace of primitive elements in the enveloping algebra. Let us compute $(\Delta\widetilde{\otimes}\mathrm{id}_{A})(R_{21} R)$ using (4.16-4.17). We have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(\Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) \left(R _ {2 1} R\right) = \left(\left(\mathrm {i d} _ {A} \widetilde {\otimes} \Delta\right) (R)\right) _ {3 1 2} \left(\Delta \widetilde {\otimes} \mathrm {i d} _ {A}\right) (R) \\ = \Phi^ {- 1} R _ {3 2} \Phi_ {1 3 2} R _ {3 1} \left(\Phi_ {3 1 2}\right) ^ {- 1} \Phi_ {3 1 2} R _ {1 3} \left(\Phi_ {1 3 2}\right) ^ {- 1} R _ {2 3} \Phi . \\ \end{array}
$$

Identifying the coefficients of h, we get

$$
\left(\Delta_ {0} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) (t) = t _ {1 3} + t _ {2 3}.
$$

(5.13)

Now write $t=\sum_{i} x_{i}\otimes y_{i}$ where $(y_{i})_{i}$ is a family of linearly independent elements of $U(\mathfrak{g})$ . Thus (5.13) becomes

$$
\sum_ {i} \Delta_ {0} \left(x _ {i}\right) \otimes y _ {i} = \sum_ {i} \left(x _ {i} \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes x _ {i}\right) \otimes y _ {i},
$$

(5.14)

(5.14)

which implies that $\Delta_{0} ( x_{i})=x_{i}\otimes1+1\otimes x_{i}$ for all i. Since the element $x_{i}$ is primitive for the comultiplication $\Delta_{0}$ of $U (\mathfrak{g})$ , it belongs to $\mathfrak{g}$ . Consequently, t belongs to $\mathfrak{g}\otimes U\mathfrak{g}$ . Relation (5.12) implies actually that t is in $\mathfrak{g}\otimes\mathfrak{g}$ .

Let us check the invariance of t. By (4.15) applied twice, we get

$$
\Delta (a) R _ {2 1} R = R _ {2 1} R \Delta (a)
$$

(5.15)

for all $a \in A.$ Identifying the coefficients of h, we obtain $\Delta_{0}(x)t=t\Delta_{0}(x)$

for all $x \in \mathfrak{g}.$

Finally, let us apply a gauge transformation $F$ to $A.$ Then by (XV.3.9) we have

$$
\left(R _ {F}\right) _ {2 1} R _ {F} = F R _ {2 1} F _ {2 1} ^ {- 1} F _ {2 1} R F ^ {- 1} = F R _ {2 1} R F ^ {- 1}.
$$

(5.16)

Taking the coefficients of h, we get $t_{F}=t$ where $t_{F}$ is the canonical 2-tensor of the QUE $A_{F}$ obtained from A by the gauge-transformation F.

At this point, the only explicit quantum enveloping algebras for a given Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ we know are the trivial QUE $U(\mathfrak{g})[[h]]$ constructed from $U(\mathfrak{g})$ as explained in Example 3 of Section 4 and their gauge-transforms. Since the universal $R$ -matrix of such a QUE is $1\otimes 1$ , the corresponding canonical 2-tensor vanishes: $t=0.$

We now present an example of a QUE with a non-zero canonical 2-tensor. We shall see more non-trivial examples in Chapters XVII and XIX.

Example 1. (A quantum enveloping algebra associated to the Heisenberg Lie algebra) We consider the 3-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ with the set $\{x,y,z\}$ as a basis and with Lie bracket determined by

$$
[ x, y ] = z \quad \text {a n d} \quad [ x, z ] = [ y, z ] = 0.
$$

$$
[ x, y ] = z \quad \text {a n d} \quad [ x, z ] = [ y, z ] = 0.
$$

The symmetric 2-tensor $t=z\otimes z$ is invariant because $z$ is central in the Lie algebra. We claim that there exists a QUE whose classical limit is $(\mathfrak{g}, t)$. Indeed, take the trivial bialgebra $A=U(\mathfrak{g})[[h]]$ as in Example 3 of Section 4, except that we set $R=e^{ht/2}$ and $\Phi=1\otimes 1\otimes 1$ . In order to make sure that $A$ is a topological braided bialgebra, we have to check Relations (4.15-4.17). The first one follows from the fact that $t$ is invariant. Relations (4.16-4.17) with $\Phi=1\otimes 1\otimes 1$ are equivalent to

$$
e ^ {h \left(t _ {1 3} + t _ {1 2}\right) / 2} = e ^ {h t _ {1 3} / 2} e ^ {h t _ {1 2} / 2} \quad \text {a n d} \quad e ^ {h \left(t _ {1 3} + t _ {2 3}\right) / 2} = e ^ {h t _ {1 3} / 2} e ^ {h t _ {2 3} / 2}.
$$

(5.17)

Relations (5.17) hold because the elements $t_{12},$ $t_{13}$ and $t_{23}$ commute with one another, due to the centrality of z. Now,

$$
R _ {2 1} R = e ^ {h t} \equiv 1 \otimes 1 + h t \pmod {h ^ {2}}
$$

shows that $t=z\otimes z$ is the canonical 2-tensor of A.

## XVI.6 Symmetrizing the Universal R-Matrix

The aim of this section is to prove that the universal R-matrix R of a quantum enveloping algebra will always satisfy $R=R_{2 1}$ after a suitable gauge transformation. We start with the following technical result.

Lemma XVI.6.1. Let A be a topological algebra which is a topologically free module. Given an element $a\in A$, there exists a unique family $(c_{n})_{n > 0}$ of complex numbers such that

$$
\left(1 + \sum_ {n > 0} c _ {n} a ^ {n} h ^ {n}\right) ^ {2} = 1 + a h.
$$

(6.1)

PROOF. Any formal series $1+\sum_{n>0} c_{n} a^{n} h^{n}$ of the above form defines an element of the inverse limit $\widetilde{A}=\varprogerright_{n} A / h^{n} A$ , hence of A since $A\cong \widetilde{A}$ by hypothesis. Equation (6.1) is equivalent to the system of equations

$$
2 c _ {1} = 1 \quad \text {a n d} \quad 2 c _ {n} + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {n - 1} c _ {p} c _ {n - p} = 0
$$

(6.2)

if n > 1. This system has a unique solution as can be seen by an easy induction.

The unique element $1+\sum_{n>0} c_{n} a^{n} h^{n}$ satisfying (6.1) is called the square root of the element $1+ah$ and is denoted by $(1+ah)^{1/2}.$ Its inverse will be denoted by $(1+ah)^{-1/2}.$

The inverse limit of any inverse system $( A_{n}, p_{n} )$ possesses a natural topology called the inverse limit topology. It is obtained as follows. In Part I we have investigated at length the quantum enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak{sl} (2)$ .
